Otamatone為電子合成器，聲音由頭部「嘴巴」內的揚聲器發出，音色可與特雷門: The Otamatone is an electronic synthesizer; the sound comes from a speaker inside the head, the "mouth", and its timbre has been compared to the theremin or the jinghu, being softer and more voice-like than the theremin's purely electronic tone. Pitch is set by sliding continuously along a logarithmic ribbon controller on the stem: the higher up you go, the lower the pitch, and the intervals between high notes are shorter than between low notes. A switch behind the head changes octave and volume. Squeezing the head opens and closes the mouth for a wah effect, and shaking the neck gives vibrato. Beside the Stylophone it has no fixed keys but a touch strip for continuous pitch change; beside a general synthesizer, its controls are reduced to a single ribbon controller and the filtering of the mouth.

Otamatone由日本明和電機與玩具公司合作開發，2009年12月1日起發售，: The Otamatone was developed by the Japanese company Maywa Denki with a toy company and went on sale on 1 December 2009. It first appeared as a toy, combining electronic music with playful product design. It was popular early on in Japan for its look and its humour, and was linked to experimental music and performance art. In 2010 it was listed among the Japan Toy Awards. In December 2019, for its tenth anniversary, an official website and social accounts were opened. In the mid-2010s it drew international attention through video platforms, cover versions and internet memes, and in 2021 Juanjo Monserrat played "Nessun dorma" from Puccini's Turandot on it at an audition for the Spanish edition of Got Talent, taking the golden buzzer after the judges tried the instrument. Versions differ in size, timbre and features; some offer volume, octave or digital connections.

Playing takes both hands: one holds and squeezes the head to open and close the mouth for a wah effect, while the other slides along the ribbon controller on the stem to set the pitch, higher up giving a lower note, with logarithmic spacing like a string instrument. 演奏Otamatone需兩手：一手握住圓頭並擠壓，聲音從頭部「嘴巴」發出；另一手: Playing the Otamatone takes both hands: one holds the round head and squeezes it, and the sound comes from the "mouth" in the head; the fingers of the other hand touch the ribbon controller on the stem and slide up and down to change pitch, higher up giving a lower note. Squeezing the head opens and closes the mouth for a wah effect, and shaking the neck gives vibrato. The switch behind the head turns it on and off and sets octave and volume. To begin, fit dry cells, hold the head steady in one hand and move slowly along the ribbon controller with the other, practising smooth pitch changes before adding the squeeze and the shake.
